title: The Almoravids and Almohads
hook: reforming movements from the Sahara and the Atlas that ruled North Africa and Spain

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Khaldun, and his idea that hardship binds a people and comfort loosens them. Your line was: bonds build, luxury loosens. Which bond did you strengthen? Day nine hundred fifty-two.

Ibn Khaldun wrote the history of two movements from his own corner of the world. First, out of the Sahara: a preacher among desert tribes, men who veil their faces, a small band devoted to prayer and strict living. In time they rule from the desert to al-Andalus. Then, out of the Atlas Mountains: another preacher, another band, sure the rulers have gone soft, who sweep down and replace them. Two waves of renewal, each coming in from the edge, each carrying the same promise: we'll bring things back to how they should be. Today: the Almoravids and Almohads.
screen: `OUT OF THE SAHARA.` → `OUT OF THE ATLAS MOUNTAINS.` → `TWO WAVES OF RENEWAL.`

segments.voice: The Almoravids, in Arabic al-Murabitun, began with a teacher named Abd Allah ibn Yasin preaching among the Sanhaja Berbers of the Sahara. Tradition ties the name to the ribat, a fortified retreat where people lived for prayer and for defense. Their strength was discipline and the Maliki law, followed closely. They founded Marrakesh, and under Yusuf ibn Tashfin they crossed the sea when Muslim rulers in al-Andalus, under pressure from Christian kingdoms to the north, asked for help. The Almohads, al-Muwahhidun, took a name meaning those who affirm the oneness of God. Their founder, Ibn Tumart, preached in the Atlas that the Almoravids had grown too fond of law books and too lax in faith. His followers took Marrakesh and became the new rulers of North Africa and al-Andalus. Under them, a philosopher you met earlier this year, Ibn Rushd, served as a judge and physician. Here is the honest part. Both movements began as calls to renewal, and both were strict. The Almohad years in particular were hard for Jews and Christians in their lands, and some families left. And both, in their turn, softened, divided, and were replaced. Ibn Khaldun, who wrote their history, saw his pattern in it. The Qur'an speaks of a community that calls others to good. In Pickthall's translation: "And there may spring from you a nation who invite to goodness, and enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency." A movement can take a verse like that as its calling. Ibn Khaldun's history asks what comes after: whether the bond that carried a movement to power holds once it is there.
screen: `AL-MURABITUN — THE PEOPLE OF THE RIBAT.` · `AL-MUWAHHIDUN — THE ONENESS OF GOD.` · `STRICT, AND HARD ON OTHERS.` · `EACH SOFTENS AND IS REPLACED.` · then, large: `RENEWAL FROM THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about reform. Settle, and breathe. This week took us from Cairo's founding through al-Azhar, Ibn Tulun's stair, the madrasah, the traveler, Ibn Khaldun, and now two reformers' movements. Bring to mind one thing in your own life that has grown soft or careless and needs renewing: a habit, a promise, a prayer you've let slide. Then ask a second question: could you renew it without turning hard on the people around you? If you pray, you can ask for renewal with humility. If you don't, choose one small thing to begin again. The bell holds the time.
Tawhid. The affirming of God's oneness that named the Almohads, one of two reforming movements, with the Almoravids, that ruled North Africa and al-Andalus in turn. Today's word.
Your line: renewal from the desert. Today, begin one thing again, and begin it gently. That closes the week. Day nine hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: The Almoravids and Almohads are remembered in North Africa through cities and buildings such as Marrakesh, and through the Maliki law and the teaching of tawhid that each emphasized.
